tier_reason: Third-party JMH benchmark (FFTBench, README plus linked run log) with public code, JDK 1.8.0_111, JVM options and an AMD Phenom II X4 955 named in the run-log file name, which would otherwise be A-level; but the FFTW baseline is the benchmark author's own ezFFTW wrapper, which builds and destroys an FFTW_ESTIMATE split-array guru plan inside every timed call under a global planner lock, and the native FFTW build is unstated, so the baseline is handicapped and the entry is held at C (analogous to the debug-baseline cap).

corrections.workload: Java JMH benchmark in the third-party FFTBench repo (JMH 1.21, JTransforms 3.1 vs ezFFTW 0.1.2): full real-to-complex forward FFT, zero the DC bin, then inverse FFT, for 1-D (1,024 to 10,000,000 elements), 2-D (1280x720 to 5000x5000) and 3-D (100x120x140 to 400x300x200) arrays, as single calls (arrayInput/singleArrayInput) and as parallel invocations.
corrections.claimed_speedup: FFTBench README (s/op, 3 JMH iterations; 2 for 3-D): 1-D arrayInput, JTransforms with its heuristic multithreading vs single-threaded ezFFTW/FFTW: 10,000,000 elements 3.205 vs 4.560; 1,024 about 1e-4 vs 0.006 (FFTW error +-0.053); FFTW faster at 98,304 (0.029 vs 0.033), 589,829 (0.815 vs 1.052) and 1,000,000 (0.175 vs 0.290). 2-D singleArrayInput with JTransforms threading disabled (snglthrd_JT) vs FFTW: 1280x720 0.137 vs 0.155, 1920x1080 0.331 vs 0.360, 3000x2000 1.100 vs 1.374, 5000x5000 6.033 vs 8.422, but 1087x1931 2.132 vs 0.998 (FFTW 2.1x faster); multithreaded JTransforms 0.058 at 1280x720 and 0.125 at 1920x1080. 3-D single-threaded: 256^3 2.272 vs 4.252, but FFTW faster at 100x120x140 (0.176 vs 0.311) and 400x300x200 (2.955 vs 4.277).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: JMH 1.21 on Oracle JDK 1.8.0_111 (HotSpot 64-Bit Server VM 25.111-b14); VM options none for the 1-D runs and -Xmx6g -Xms3g for the 2-D and 3-D runs (per the linked run log); native FFTW comes from the bytedeco JavaCPP preset via ezFFTW, build and version not stated
corrections.hardware: AMD Phenom II X4 955 on Ubuntu 16.04 (from the run-log file name runs/ubuntu_16.04_phenom_II_x4_955.txt)
corrections.stars_or_usage: 430 stars, 94 forks; version 3.2 on Maven Central
corrections.caveats: Mixed result: the benchmark author's own conclusion is that no library wins everywhere. FFTW is reached through ezFFTW (GPL-2.0, written by the benchmark's author), which creates an FFTW_ESTIMATE plan, executes and destroys it on every call inside the timed operation, serializes planning behind a global lock, uses the split-array guru interface and copies data through JNI, so the baseline is far from tuned FFTW (the 1,024-point 0.006 s figure is overhead, not FFT time). The 1-D JTransforms rows have JTransforms' multithreading enabled while FFTW is single-threaded; in like-for-like single-threaded 2-D and 3-D runs the results split both ways. Hardware is a 2009-era AMD Phenom II on Java 8; each JMH row used only 2-3 iterations and some error bars exceed the score. The JTransforms README itself shows no FFTW numbers. Pure Java, not C++.

notes: Numbers in the record match the FFTBench README exactly; corrections add the threading split, the 3-D results, the JVM/CPU details found in the linked run log, and the ezFFTW per-call FFTW_ESTIMATE planning found in its FFTW_Guru.java. JTransforms BSD-2-Clause, 430 stars, last commit 2025-12-05 confirmed (active).

tier_reason: A single GitHub issue (#165, 2017-04-20) lists 'Cycles' for five FFT libraries on one phone at one size with no code, compiler, Ne10 version or methodology; numbers without methodology are C.

corrections.workload: Complex FFT of length 1024 on an Android Samsung Galaxy S6, 'Cycles' per library, posted in Ne10 GitHub issue #165 ('Ne10 vs Superpowered', 2017-04-20) by GitHub user lieff, who writes 'we made some fft benchmarks' and does not claim to have written any of the libraries.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Issue #165 table ('Cycles', unit and measurement method not explained): SuperpoweredFFT 7375; ne10_fft (asm) 10125; libavcodec (asm) 14375; tricl_fft_fft 21833; CkFft 25000. So Ne10 is about 1.42x faster than libavcodec (derived from page data) and SuperpoweredFFT is about 1.37x faster than Ne10 (derived from page data). The issue says further optimization of Ne10 is possible.
corrections.caveats: Weak evidence: one issue post with one size, one phone, no code and no methodology or Ne10 version; the 'Cycles' unit is not defined. The record previously said the measurement came from SuperpoweredFFT's author; the issue does not say that. It does not compare to KissFFT or FFTW. Ne10's own ARM community blog posts reportedly compare against FFTW, OpenMax DL, kissFFT and pffft (search snippets say Ne10 beats FFTW in most cases), but developer.arm.com is blocked here, so those numbers are not recorded; a dlib discussion (#3030) says Ne10 FFTs are much faster than FFTW on ARM but gives no numbers. Last commit 2018-11-15.

notes: Issue numbers confirmed verbatim; misattribution of the poster corrected. BSD-3-Clause (ARM Limited) confirmed from LICENSE; 1.5k stars; last commit 2018-11-15 on master (abandoned). A better tier needs the ARM blog benchmark page, which a non-cloud run could open.
